name: Dihydroquercetin glucoside
lead: Dihydroquercetin glucoside (DHQG) is described in hair-care marketing as one of the two components of Redensyl, a cosmetic active added to scalp serums and lotions with the aim of supporting hair growth and a fuller-looking head of hair; the other component is EGCG-glucoside. Users apply Redensyl-type serums to the scalp for months, hoping for thicker-looking hair and less visible thinning. DHQG is a glucoside of dihydroquercetin, also called taxifolin, a flavanonol found in Siberian larch, milk thistle and other plants [1].

No clinical study of DHQG on its own has been published. It has been tested only as part of finished products: a 2020 randomized, single-blinded, vehicle-controlled study of a lotion combining Redensyl and Sepicontrol A5 in 44 people with androgenetic alopecia reported improvements, and a 2025 open-label study of a rosemary and Redensyl serum in healthy women evaluated hair outcomes for a multi-ingredient product [2][3]. A 2025 review discusses Redensyl among topical hair actives [4].

chain: Redensyl-type serum applied to the scalp
Marketed to support follicle activity and the growth phase
angle.text: People use serums containing DHQG as part of the Redensyl blend hoping for thicker-looking hair. Trial results are for finished multi-ingredient products rather than DHQG alone.

infobox: Siberian larch, milk thistle (silymarin), other plants [1]

paras: Taxifolin is a flavonoid polyphenol. Wikipedia lists natural sources including Siberian larch and other conifers, the silymarin extract of milk thistle seeds, vinegars aged in cherry wood, and plant foods such as fruit, vegetables, wine, tea and cocoa, and notes it also occurs as glycosides such as astilbin in acai and red onions [1].

Preclinical findings summarised there include that taxifolin was reported as not mutagenic and less toxic than quercetin, was proposed as a chemopreventive agent, may stimulate collagen fibril formation, and in one cosmetic study inhibited melanogenesis about as effectively as arbutin; the article does not mention hair [1]. DHQG itself is the glucoside form used in the Redensyl blend.

DHQG is sold as part of Redensyl in over-the-counter scalp serums and lotions, usually alongside other actives. Marketing describes Redensyl as supporting follicle regeneration and hair density, a description repeated in the 2025 serum study [3].

A 2020 trial of a Redensyl and Sepicontrol A5 lotion used twice daily for 24 weeks randomized 44 patients to active or vehicle; of 26 active-treated patients, 7.7 percent had great improvement, 73.1 percent moderate improvement and 19.2 percent remained stable, with the median anagen-to-telogen ratio rising from 2.25 to 6.02 and no significant adverse events reported [2]. Because the lotion contained more than one active, results cannot be assigned to DHQG itself.

No studies found for DHQG alone. A randomized, single-blinded, vehicle-controlled study of a Redensyl and Sepicontrol A5 lotion in 44 patients with androgenetic alopecia reported improvement over 24 weeks; 41 patients (18 men and 23 women) completed it, and quality-of-life scores and self-assessment improved [2].

A 2025 open-label, single-arm study of the Soulflower Rosemary Redensyl serum in healthy women measured hair growth rate, length, density, thickness, anagen-to-telogen ratio, hair fall and graying over 120 days using phototrichogram and comb tests. The authors reported increases in growth rate (46.71 percent by day 90), density (37.92 percent) and thickness (80.85 percent by day 120) and reductions in hair fall and graying, with no adverse effects; the serum also contained other ingredients including rice water, chia seed extract, rosemary oil, MelanoGray and AnaGain [3].

A 2025 review of topical hair actives, covering Redensyl, Procapil, Capixyl, Baicapil, AnaGain, onion juice, coffee extract, saw palmetto, pumpkin seed oil and rosemary oil, found these were mostly studied as combined formulations in randomized trials or prospective cohorts with promising results, while noting limited sample sizes, lack of comparison with standard therapies, differences between study groups, undisclosed alopecia types and conflicts of interest [4].

Redensyl-containing serums are sold widely as cosmetics, and social media marketing for hair-growth serums is discussed in the 2025 review, which describes sponsored promotion of these products on social media [4]. Because they are cosmetics rather than drugs, they are generally promoted as add-ons to, or alternatives for people who do not tolerate, standard hair-loss therapies; the review states that these topicals have a less significant side-effect profile [4].

timeline.event: Randomized, single-blinded, vehicle-controlled study of a Redensyl and Sepicontrol A5 lotion in 44 people with androgenetic alopecia is published [2].
Open-label serum study and a review of topical hair actives are published [3][4].

card.summary: A taxifolin derivative in Redensyl; no studies of it on its own.

quick.overview:
DHQG is a sugar-linked form of taxifolin, a plant flavonoid. In marketing it is one half of the Redensyl hair-growth active.
No study of DHQG alone was found; small studies test finished serums.
quick.mechanism: Taxifolin has laboratory findings in unrelated areas; no hair-growth mechanism is established.
quick.risks: Taxifolin is reported as non-mutagenic in bacterial tests; no human safety data for DHQG were found.
